entities.name: Abd al-Razzaq Lahiji
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
ʿAbd-al-Razzāq b. ʿAlī b. al-Ḥosayn Lāhījī (died 1662), known by his pen name Fayyāż ("the Giver of Abundance"), was a towering figure in 17th-century Safavid Iran, a polymath whose intellectual contributions spanned theology, philosophy, and poetry. As a prominent disciple and son-in-law of the seminal philosopher Mullā Ṣadrā, Lāhījī became a leading exponent of the School of Isfahan, solidifying and transmitting the complex metaphysical doctrines of his mentor. His work was crucial in integrating rational philosophy (ḥikmah) with mystical intuition (ʿirfān) and Shiʿi theology, thereby shaping the intellectual landscape of Persianate Islam for centuries.

Lāhījī's philosophical output, primarily written in Persian and Arabic, sought to systematize and popularize Mullā Ṣadrā's transcendent philosophy (al-ḥikma al-mutaʿāliya). His magnum opus, "Gawhar-e Morād" (The Desired Jewel), composed around 1640, is a comprehensive treatise on metaphysics, theology, ethics, and eschatology, serving as a key text for understanding Sadra's thought and earning him the epithet "Ṣadr-e Thānī" (The Second Ṣadr). Beyond philosophy, he was a respected poet, leaving behind a Dīwān that further showcased his erudition and spiritual depth.

His role as a teacher at the Madrasa-ye ʿAbdallāh Shushtarī in Qom was pivotal in institutionalizing and disseminating the philosophical insights of the School of Isfahan. Through his detailed commentaries and accessible summaries of Sadra's challenging ideas, Lāhījī ensured that Sadra's unique synthesis of Peripatetic, Illuminationist, and mystical traditions became a cornerstone of advanced religious and philosophical education in Iran. His clear expositions clarified complex concepts such as the substantial motion (ḥarakat-e jawharī) and the unity of existence (waḥdat al-wujūd), making them accessible to a wider scholarly audience.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Abd al-Razzaq Lahiji was pivotal in systematizing and transmitting the complex philosophical legacy of Mullā Ṣadrā, ensuring its enduring influence on Shiʿi thought and education for centuries. His works became foundational texts in Iranian madrasas, shaping the intellectual landscape of the region.
